utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we resume, I first have to explain to you that we had some technical problems, Mr. Bukva. Therefore, we couldn't start any earlier than -- we had a delay of one hour. We'll have to consider how to proceed, but it might be that we try to do with one break, and then perhaps if there would be time a little bit longer, we have three hours and three quarters of an hour until 7.00, so if that would be possible with the translators and the technicians, we might see whether we can do with one break, if necessary a break of 35 or even 40 minutes. Then one remark for the Defence. The Defence is aware that there's still a motion pending on the issuing of a subpoena for certain witnesses. The Chamber has taken as the Defence might be aware of some initiative in order to secure as good as possible the appearance of those witnesses in this courtroom where the Chamber considered that subpoenaing these witnesses might not be the most effective way of reaching the result. So we hope that this will give the result that the Defence would try to achieve. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you needed another few questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Very briefly, I asked Madam Registrar if we could have the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Usher could put it on the ELMO, please. We are particularly interested in the eastern part of the map. Yes, the eastern part. I said the eastern part. While what's on the screen now is the western part. May I have the eastern side, please. Could you please position the map in such a way that we can see the furthest eastern part. Again, that's western part. So eastern part is the opposite side of the western side. So if we can go further east, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The very right edge of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we make sure that we can see the lower part of that area, please. We can stop here. Thank you. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at this map carefully. Could we please have the map a little up, please. Go a bit up with the map. Stop. Stop here. Right, yes. And if you can tell us -- I'm going to ask you two questions in relation to this map. Can you tell us if on one hand you would wish to add or modify something on this map, and my question is in relation to the other map as well, the other side of the map that we had a look at a moment ago, in relation to specifically --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Counsel doesn't need to go any further with the question, could the witness be asked to remove his headphones or to step outside -- or to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will rephrase the question so that the witness does not have to leave the courtroom. With your leave, Mr. President, since the witness has already waited a long time, with your leave, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, would your objection be about the subject matter or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Subject matter. Then the witness has to leave the courtroom. Mr. Stamp, when the door is closed, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question proceeds by inviting the witness to add or modify something that he might have put on the map. He was asked to put what he knew on the map. He was asked questions about it subsequently and this was still in chief. Not in cross-examination. In chief He was asked questions in respect to a particular place, if he knew something about a particular place, he said he could not recall anything further in respect to that. In respect to positions on the map, nothing was asked in cross-examination except a church and from where a video is taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we would say the church is not on this part of the map. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked the witness whether he would like to add something to the map. Could you tell us how this comes up from the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, that's why I said immediately I wanted to rephrase my question. We believe that is the reason why I wanted to start with the eastern part of the map. We believe that the indjication or the marking done by the witness, and he was asked a question regarding Lukavica, that is, to locate where Lukavica was. So this was a question that came from the Prosecution, or the question asked by your Chamber. But in any case, in the same movement, in the same gesture, when he was circling about the church, he was asked a question about Lukavica. Now, this map, Mr. President, shows Lukavica very close to -- in between the eastern and the western part. That's why I wanted first to have a look at the eastern part in its entirety, and then I wanted to move very slowly towards the western part so he can tell us if as he was doing the exercise he perhaps may well have made a mistake by putting a cross where he had placed the cross. And we believe that he had put the cross on the facility where it said electrotechnical faculty. We all know the barracks of Lukavica are not located at the electrotechnical faculty. So that is a technical error. And what we wanted is for the witness to have a look at the map from east towards the west in order to ask him a question if there was something that perhaps he could add something from this observation, and then looking, examining the map in its entirety from east to west. And I would have asked the question precisely about whether this was true, what he has put in, what he has marked on the map. And that came from the cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I did not ask the witness to locate Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did, as far as I remember. I asked the witness when questioned about the position of the church, I asked him to indjicate on the map where the position of the barracks, or at least the structures shown on the video were located. So it -- but I have no... If the -- As a matter of fact, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, it was not about barracks, as I just said, but it was about from where the video has been taken. Yes, and that as far as I understand is the logic tells us that was at least from the premises of where the office of General Galic was situated. I think if there are good reasons to believe that a mistake was made, I'll ask the witness since it was my question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I wanted to say was that on the eastern part of the map, we can see -- we can see where it says "Lukavica" on the western part of the map -- the western part of the eastern part of the map, that's what I wanted to say, is that we can see very well that where the witness had placed the cross, the contours of the buildings as they are drawn up do not correspond to what we saw on the recording, on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me do the following: I have this map with the markings, but without the church and the last. I'll hand this to the witness and ask him to point at where the video was taken. And since I have not an eastern and a western, but I have combined them already, it would be easier for the witness. So the witness may be brought into the courtroom again. And could this map be shown to the witness. Mr. Bukva, you can hear me again. You have not yet answered any questions, so I remind you that you were still bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony. And after I have done so, could please that map be put, I'll give some instructions, a bit more to the right and a bit more up. Yes, that's the wrong direction. I should have said a bit more to the left, and a little bit down or up so that the lower part appears. A bit more even. A bit more to the -- if the map would be moved to the left so we get more side, yes a bit more even. Yes a bit more. Yes, a bit more up, please. No, the map a bit more up so that we see the lower part. Yes, that part. Mr. Bukva, what you see now is the map as you have marked it during the break. The markings you made in respect of the Orthodox church and of the position from where the video was taken do not appear on this map. Could you please point, first of all, at the Orthodox church. So if the witness could be provided with the pointer, not with a pen. Yes. You now have pointed at the Orthodox church which appears just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Next to the word Dobrinja and just above the word Autobusna Stanica. Could you again point at the position from where the video was taken. And if I understood your testimony well, you testified that the video was taken from the premises close to the office of General Galic, to be more precise, just at the corner of the building in which the offices of General Galic were situated on the first floor. Would you please point at that spot again on this map with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I know what this is about. On this map, there is not a single building of the barracks Slobodan Princip Seljo that has been put on this map. This is the road which is the so-called Bjelo Polje Road. Along that road is the barracks, that is, the fence of the barracks which takes this whole area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, yesterday we saw some cars driving on a road. Could you please point at what road that was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is this road, Mr. President, this road here. That is the main road. I believe it's the second-class road. This road here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then may I ask you, so where you marked the map yesterday, approximately where it reads "electrotechnical faculty" which I take it stands for faculty, that that was a wrong marking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, it's a mistake. I really apologise because of the problem that I caused, but I was obviously careless, and possibly I was a little tired. So I apologise again for causing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your apologies are accepted. Mr. Bukva, then, could you please indjicate with the pointer where approximately, although buildings are not reflected in this map, that where approximately at the side of this road the barracks could be found from where the video was taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, that will be a very rough way of doing it, but knowing the ground, I will try to do it as precise as possible. But it will be this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the witness now points at an area which is approximately a quarter of a centimetre to the right of a yellow road that goes from point 527 to 5.8 of the map, and it is approximately 1 to 1 and a half centimetre to the right of where he marked on the map the Orthodox church was. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I think that perhaps we could ask for -- no, not necessary. Thank you. Witness, yesterday you said also as a follow up to the questions of the Prosecution and other questions what happened when there was fog. I think that was on page 63, if my memory doesn't fail me. And the question I wanted to ask you is the following: Your answer, and you will say this is probably normal, your answer did not seem very clear to me. I would like you to tell us very precisely what you heard that was said as far as the sentry is concerned, the guards. If there is fog, and if the guards believe to see or not see what's in front of them, what was their position in relation to the opening of fire? And we're speaking about the crossing of the runway, of the airport runway.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was precise. My answer was, and I'm going to repeat it now, yesterday what I said is that if the soldiers were speaking on the line, were talking on the front line, the positions, if there was fire that is fired from our positions, and if there was a response from the runway, then our soldiers would fire on the target spotted. If this did not occur, that is, if the response on the other side did not occur, then our soldiers would not open fire. And according to what they said, they did not do that. I believe that's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But you spoke of a kind of cunning that you used at war, and you said that if a soldier believed that he could see something vaguely through the fog, and he wouldn't know what that was, that he would then employ a kind of cunning. Could you please describe what was that trick that they used? Could you please state that clearly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gave you the example that fire would be opened up in the air if people were spotted, that was what was done. And if there was a response from the other side, obviously response in firing, then it would be obvious that these were enemy soldiers that were firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, witness, I'd like you now, and it is probably going to be our last question, could we please talk about the aspect of civilian targets and military targets. You said following some questions asked on page 53 that there was a lot of care put into discerning civilian targets from military targets. And could you please elaborate on this aspect in terms of technical aspects of this bearing in mind your own knowledge and experience. Mr. Usher, Mr. President, I don't think that we will need the map any longer, so I don't think that the map needs to stay next to the witness although he can keep it if he wishes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Before the witness proceeds to answer, may I just given a citation of the quotation of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave you page 53. If you wish -- do you wish to have the exact quote?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem for the Chamber is that when we search, the next day the pages are numbered through. So if you could give some literal text, then we would be able to search for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'm going to have to reopen that. And if we look under searching for word "target," we should be able to find something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've found the words "civilian targets" on page 18.470, line 20. But that's in a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My record, and subject to corrections from the Bench, contrary to what my friend said that the witness said, that the witness that there was a lot of care put into discerning civilian targets from military targets. My record is that -- and this is at page 54, "we gathered data on enemy military facilities, not on civilian facilities. And that is what I forwarded to my superior, so there was no point in distinguishing between a civilian and a military."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's also my recollection, but please correct me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if I'm wrong, that the witness testified that since they were concentrating on military targets, that they were not -- but if I'm wrong, please find the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I would never say that you were mistaken. What I wanted to say is that the witness said that there were two categories of targets, and that there was a difference between them. That's what I'm looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your question was about a different matter. You said about specific care was taken, that's a different matter, and that's what Mr. Stamp objects against. I'll do a search for the word "care."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my expression is not always what the transcript says, thank God, in fact. And if I say that care was taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we don't want any debate on that. The question now is there has been put some doubt on whether you reflected the testimony in a proper way, that you now find the place you'd like refer to, and you put that to the witness, his testimony. What I find in the transcript is on page 18.451, and it might be that you wanted to refer to the answer of the witness on line 7 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that I must have deduced this expression "great care" from another statement that was uttered, and that's on page 54, 56 - I don't know how that's possible - but I have on my screen, page 56 of yesterday. [In English] "It was strictly observed that the actual, real targets are hit." And it was the words "strictly observed," and from then I deduced --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness testified yesterday that they strictly observed to hit the targets, but as far as the targets are concerned, the witness said that there was no point in distinguishing between a civilian and a military so there would be only data, information, on military facilities, on military equipment. So what you say, whether you hit a target or not, and when you precisely observe what happened to that, is very different from what you put to the witness right away. And what you now did as a matter of fact to start a debate in explaining why what you said was correct in view of the transcript, it is not. So Mr. Bukva, before answering the question, we'll first listen to the question. And then I'll allow you or not allow you to answer the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So Witness, you stated the following, asked by the Prosecution, you stated the following: In relation to the fire that was opened on alleged civilian populations, your interpreted answer was the following: I'm going to quote "that the actual real targets are hit." I would be grateful if you can elaborate on this, please. And if you can tell us what you meant by that. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Could you tell me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, where the question says that fire was opened on alleged civilian populations? You said that that was the question you quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not quote the question. I did not quote the question. What I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you introduced new elements which are not reflecting the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a question. When you said that you strictly observed the actual -- the real targets, could you tell us what you meant to say by that? How did you observe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I remember my answer very well as given to the Prosecution. At the very beginning of the answer, I denied his statement that civilian targets were targeted, were fired on, by saying that my service gathered data only about military targets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. It has been read. But now I am asking you about -- you said that you strictly observed that the actual real targets were hit. Could you tell us how you did that or what you exactly did, what you meant when you gave that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, under that term, "we strictly observed" took care to hit military targets. And which way this was done, this care, this attention that was given to this, at this very moment I cannot explain it because this was carried out by artillery experts, by having the real elements, coordinates, by determining the right position of the target, that I believe is the most efficient way of having all the conditions met in order to hit the actual, that is, the military, real target. That's what is included in this. So this is the right care that's taken, due attention given, so that the actual military target is hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I understand your testimony to be that every care was taken that you would target as precisely in order to hit the target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Nieto-Navia has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you didn't recall about any military targets at Alipasino Polje. But after that, you said that probably there was a workshop, and you had pointed it out on the map yesterday. I would like you to see the map again. That part is the eastern part -- the official one, yes. The western part. Yes, that part. Thank you. That's okay. Below that, please. Can you see the Novi Grad name, put that in the centre, please. The map a little bit -- that's okay. That's okay. Perfect. Do you see the flag in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indjicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: And the letters KM, as far as I remember, meant command post.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You said that "we pointed out on the map yesterday." But I cannot see where there is a workshop at Alipasino Polje. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If you remember, I immediately said that it was a problem of locating a certain part of the town. I said it was -- I said a weapons factory was near Alipasino, and it was in the Zica factory. But this has to do with Alipasino bridge, Alipasin Most, not Alipasino Polje. So if we could move the map a little bit down, then it would be visible. We do have Alipasino Polje here, but further above we have Alipasin Most, Alipasino bridge. You can see it here. And in the immediate vicinity, we have the letter R. This is the Zica factory where there was a workshop of ammunition and weapons. There was a prewar factory here. The prewar Zica factory, so we have Alipasin Most and Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. Can I take it that at Alipasino Polje, there were no workshops as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to information on the map, you are right. There was nothing -- there was no factory for ammunition, weapons, in Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I would like to make sure that I have understood you correctly. My first question is in order to clarify something that you mentioned in the course of your testimony. You said, and I'll quote you in English. You very briefly said that you are well informed about the enemy side. You said that you had information about what was happening on the enemy side. That is what you said, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In our opinion, we did have reliable information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question has to do with whether you were familiar with the state of morale, with the psychological state that was prevalent on the enemy side. And perhaps I'll clarify that a little more. I think that all the sides in the conflict have an interest in using or in conducting what is also called a psychological war. You said that the enemy side also used the media. And you said that they also used CNN or other chains. So my question has to do with whether you were familiar with the state of morale, with the psychological state on the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the field of operations and the tasks that the intelligence department had, given these tasks, given these field of operations, I will restrict my answer to the military aspect. And my answer could be as follows: We also gathered that kind of information about enemy manpower. And that is to say about the BH army, and I'll repeat what I said yesterday: All information on enemy manpower was important for us as this is an element that has a direct influence on our own forces in the sense that it was necessary to take preventive measures to obstruct such an influence and to prevent surprises from occurring. I would also like to add that in general, army morale is a very interesting matter for intelligence departments, and it is something that is very difficult to assess in the case of the enemy. But it's of great importance for the way events unfold on the battlefield. We had certain intelligence, information about morale, and we attempted to gather such information. As to how reliable, how complete this information was, that would require a special analysis. But I would like to repeat that I have only spoken about the morale of the enemy army here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well. So you are saying that you were familiar with the state of morale of the enemy forces on the basis of your analysis. Can you tell us in rough terms, if we talk about the September 1992, to the end of the summer 1994 period, was state of morale deteriorating then or was it more or less at the same level? Were you able to influence the state of morale? Were you able to affect the psychological state of the enemy side, yes or no? Did you succeed in doing so? Did you have other methods which would enable you to act in this manner, in this field? Could you perhaps clarify this a little for me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "you," I suppose you are referring to the department whose head I was. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any particular means which would enable us to carry out psychological and propaganda activity. So in that sense, we didn't do anything in particular. We didn't act in any particular way. But if you're asking me which methods we used to affect the combat morale of the enemy army, then I can tell you this: The Lukavac 93 operation in which the enemy suffered great casualties and it was a great defeat, this was the best means of diminishing the morale of the enemy army. The victories of our army on the front always had a good effect on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, because you mentioned Lukavac 1993, and that was the second question I wanted to put to you. Could you very briefly tell me what the strategic objective of this plan was, because if I have understood you correctly, you said that the attack or the operation was stopped because the UN intervened. Could you briefly explain to me what the strategic objective was and how you were able to implement this objective in order to have strategic success, tactical success.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had an operational objective, not a strategic objective. Yesterday I already said that the main staff led this operation. In addition to the SRK, other units from the Republika Srpska army participated in this operation, so the operational objective of this operation was to reduce the length of the front of the SRK. Because as I said yesterday, I'd like to remind you of this, I spoke about the ratio of forces. I said it was -- the ratio was 4 to 1 with regard to the enemy, in relation to the enemy. As far as I know, the objective of this operation was to reduce the length of the SRK's front, and then to liberate Trnovo so that the eastern and western part of Republika Srpska could be joined up, or rather the territory under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. So the objective was to join the eastern and western parts of those -- of that territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what means did you use? You said that the ratio of your forces to enemy forces was 1 to 4. It wasn't in your favour. In order to fight against this disadvantage, in order to find a remedy to this disadvantage, could you tell me, what were your thoughts? How did you act? What did you do to improve your situation? I don't want you to go into details, but I'm interested in the principle on which this plan was based. If we bear in mind the restricted number of your forces which didn't allow you to engage in a direct conflict, but please correct me if I'm mistaken in presenting things in this way.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I personally did not participate in the planning of this operation. And your question isn't quite clear to me. I apologise. But I can't really see what you want to find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll put that question to you again. But if possible, I'd like a very brief answer. My question has to do with the principle on which this operation was based, given the context, given your disadvantage in the sense that you -- your forces were not as strong, your forces in comparison to the number of enemy troops were not as strong. The ratio was 1 to 4. According to your military position, how did you intend to counter this disadvantage? I don't know if I have been clear. I'm not a military man; I'm not a soldier. But I am trying to express myself all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's a technical problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Purely technical. I don't think that the words "according to your military position" were translated by the Serbian booth and this could be important. No, for the Serb booth, the words that I will quote now: "According to your military position," I don't think these words were translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's a problem with the transcript. But you can answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I really don't know what I should answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer my question, if you can remember my question. Mr. Piletta-Zanin mentioned a transcript problem. This does not concern you directly. You heard my question, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So in military terms if that's right, if an offensive is being planned, and the action taken was of an offensive kind, in such cases, you take into account the main elements that are required in order to achieve the objective. And the relation of forces which is very important, if an attack or defence is concerned, is something that the commander determines. He determines the focus of the military action. If it's an attack, the focus of the attack. If it's a defence, the focus of the defence. And he also determines what the concentration of forces will be in a certain direction. So, if you have understood me, I already said that in addition to the SRK forces, other forces from the Army of Republika Srpska participated. And in this way, at the very beginning, our disadvantage, as far as manpower is concerned, wasn't so serious. That's the first thing. The second thing is the optimal direction of the attack. You have to determine where the enemy is at his weakest, and that is the point which one will attack with one's own forces, with strong forces. And this is how one breaks through the enemy front, and then one takes advantage of this breakthrough by taking well-known tactical action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a little question I want to ask you. You said that you yourself were a target for snipers. You yourself came under sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean? How did you know that fire was opened by a sniper? How did you know that it was sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was in such a place and at such a distance that it was possible to conclude that it was a sniper. In one case, fragmentation ammunition was used, and only sniper rifles use such ammunition. To be more specific, part of the Lukavac/Pale Road in the Osmice area, for a certain period of time, about 50 metres -- a 50-metre section of that road was not protected, and it came under sniper fire. They would open fire on that part of the road. And that is where I was shot at. I didn't mention the first occasion. That was in the barracks itself in the area of the the Vranjis elevation, and the third time was in Grbavica. That is to say in the urban part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But very briefly, how far away was the sniper very roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about how snipers took action, how they fired. I think it's difficult to determine this, because it's difficult to spot snipers. But let's say on Grbavica, I know that part of town very well. It couldn't have been at a distance exceeding 300 metres. But as far as the case in the barracks is concerned, I couldn't really say, but I'm sure that it came from the direction of Dobrinja, from a highrise building. Perhaps one could say that it was from a distance of between four and five hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And you said that it was possible for you to come to the conclusion that it was a sniper on the basis of the bullets. You saw the fragments, the dum dum ammunition, if I have understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't see those fragments. You are talking about bullet fragments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you said that you were fired on by a sniper. Why didn't you say it was an ordinary soldier who shot at you? Why did you say that it was a sniper?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, it's the type of ammunition used that led me to that conclusion. I said that the ammunition used was a fragmentation ammunition, fragmentation bullets or the so-called dum dum bullets. When I mentioned the event in the barracks when a sniper shot at me, I saw that the bullet came from my rear. It missed me, and it hit an obstacle which was 2 or 3 metres in front of me. When it hit that obstacle, the fragmentation bullet, the dum dum bullet, was activated. It exploded. You understand. And the same thing happened when I was exposed to sniper fire on Grbavica. The bullet hit the road and it exploded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But are these bullets necessarily used by sniper rifles or can a sniper use other bullets which are not necessarily dum dum bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not such an expert, but I know that various types of ammunition are used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My very last question, then: You said, if I've understood you correctly, you said that the BH army based itself on the model of the former JNA, that its structure was based on the former JNA model. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So does this remark also apply to your army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The same rules were applied. Or rather the organisation, the establishment, it was the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So within the JNA army, were there sniper units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no special sniper units, no. Exclusively sniper units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, or rather were there snipers who were part of other units, attached to other units? So units where there were two or three or a certain number of snipers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it states in the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, I have some questions for you as well. First, you made a comparison between the strength of your troops, and you also compared the number of infantry weapons available to the opposing party and your forces. You told us that they had far more troops and far more infantry weapons. Would the same be true for heavy weapons? Would they have more heavy weapons than you had? Would they have approximately the same number, or would they have less?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's difficult to answer this question very precisely. I was not in a position to be able to say how many such heavy weapons remained in the barracks of the former JNA because in Sarajevo and in the surroundings of Sarajevo, and this had an important effect on the balance of forces, one of the conditions for them to withdraw from barracks in Sarajevo, one of the conditions was to leave all the heavy weapons in the barracks, and this was done. I don't have any precise information. But at the end of the war, the relation was more or less the same. It was more or less equal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said at the end of the war. During the war, what was your global perception of the availability of having heavy weapons compared in your forces and the opposite forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you a precise answer. It's a very delicate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's why I asked you the question, since you seem to be very well aware of the comparison between the number of troops and the number of infantry weapons. So I thought you might have some knowledge about heavy weapons as well. My next question to you is: Are you aware of any military courts or court martials functioning during the war within the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although this is not my field of expertise, I am aware that military courts did exist, but these were regular military courts. And I'd just like to say in relation to this that the authorities of Republika Srpska had never declared a state of war. So it was the peacetime laws that were applied. And in relation to that, military regular courts existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are under some time restraints. So I asked you whether you were aware, and you said yes, I was. There were military courts, but not a court working in accordance with the state of war, but just as if it were peace. Could you tell us where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one such court was located in Ilidza, at Ilidza, that part of Sarajevo under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm specifically asking about a military court functioning in the SRK. Since you said it was under the control of the Army of the Republika Srpska, that's not exactly the same. Could you please tell us whether it was within the -- within your corps or outside your corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this court was located at Ilidza on the territory of Ilidza. But all military courts were under the immediate or control of the Ministry of Defence. They were part of the Ministry of Defence. They were not part of the corps. So the military judiciary was part of the Ministry of Defence of the army of Republika Srpska. Such a court was located at Ilidza. One such court was in Nevesinje as far as I recall, and one such court was located in Bijeljina. So these courts were established according to territorial principle, and they were all part of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know of any case of a suspect or an accused to be from within the SRK to be sent to any of these courts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yesterday we mentioned the paramilitary unit St. George. And if you remember, I said that they ended up in court. And as far as some individual cases are concerned, I wouldn't be able to remember because that was under the strict authority of the military judiciary. And I really had no direct connection with them at all. But what I've said in relation to the St. George's group, I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was, if I did understand you well, a matter of insubordination or...?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spoke about the St. George's group as a -- one of the paramilitary units. And because of having committed murder, because of looting and robbery, they had to appear in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they appear in the military court?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question is: You told us about the existence of workshops. What happened with those workshops? And I'm talking about workshops where ammunition or at least military products were produced or repaired. What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Mr. President. Perhaps it's the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they destroyed? Were they left alone? Were they observed by you just in order to see what production they were capable of doing? Or what happened to it? What did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I said that the duty and obligation of my service was to gather such information, such intelligence, and to forward them to the command. And measures taken by the command, I wouldn't be aware of them. In a sense, whether anything was undertaken against those, I don't know. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you have a relatively precise knowledge of the existence of such workshops, would it not be part of your intelligence tasks to see whether they continued to exist? So wouldn't you therefore not know if they would have been destroyed or moved to another place? So that's why I'm asking you what happened to these workshops.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I wasn't sure whether they were fired at, whether anything was done. But considering it all, we did follow their activity and it is true that during the war they changed location. And we followed the activity of those workshops. And for us, this activity was always of interest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And any change of location, did that ever happened due to the workshop being destroyed by military action or damaged by military action?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said there were mujahedin in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what you mean by that and how you would know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Mujahedin are people who came from Islamic countries and took part in fighting the Serbs on the side of the Muslims. The information on the presence of the Mujahedin, we received this in several ways. But the most secure way was from people who crossed over to our territory and possibly from people who were exchanged from those areas. So we would learn this from people who saw that, who saw them, who saw the Mujahedin in those areas. And the unit that was present there, the El Fatah unit consisted of about 150 Mujahedin, exclusively Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this is, I would say, imported manpower in the troops of the opposite army. Did you have any import of abroad or -- well, let's say, outside the area who would be incorporated in your troops either temporary or a permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual cases. You cannot speak of a whole unit exclusively. You cannot speak about an exclusive unit, say, from Yugoslavia, to take an example. But there were individual cases. These were volunteers. As far as I recall, there were, but not many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were also subordinated to the command of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were part of the regular units of the corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You told us in respect of one of the documents shown to you that you did remember the day very well because one of the mortar shells of which this report -- mentioned in this report, you said, "fell in a prison where prisoners were walking in the morning." Were you in that prison when that shell fell?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this from talking to someone. I can't quite remember the name. I think a prison guard who was a friend of mine, an acquaintance of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you more or less by accident learned about it, not as a part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about the event. I knew about the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember how much later you found out about the event?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same day. Do you remember when it was exactly? What day it was or what month?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: September of what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then my next question is you have been -- questions have been put to you in respect of whether something happened as a -- as they call it in French, a barrage of fire, a lot of weaponry firing at the same time for at least 20 minutes, at Christmas either 24th or 25th of December, either the 6th or the 7th of January, 1992/1993. You said you were not aware of such event?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there anything else special at either the December Christmas or the January Christmas that you noticed? I mean, was there something like such a thing but for a shorter period of time, or was there any special in respect of firing at one of these Christmas Days or Christmas Eves?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you told us about Markale. Do you know whether the Markale incident where it was alleged that a marketplace was hit by a shell, do you know whether any investigation was done by a group inside your Sarajevo Romanija Corps? So I'm not talking about a mixed group, but...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question. I understood it. What you mean is an investigation as part of our forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether a group was formed for that or whether it happened and how it was organised, if it happened.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain that there was a team that was established on the orders of the commander. But I do know that certain measures were taken in order to ascertain, to ascertain whether this mortar shell, as this was alleged, whether this mortar shell came from our positions. These measures were taken to find this out in all the units of the SRK, particularly in relation to the units that were, for instance, in the area from which it would have been possible to fire this. However, I have to remind you that at that time, there was a ban on firing from weapons of a calibre above 12.7 millimetre, or perhaps that such weapons were even elsewhere. They were dislocated, put on some other locations. And there were certain investigative measures that were taken, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A ban by whom? Are you referring to the establishment of the exclusion zone, the total exclusion zone, or any other ban?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a ban on firing from weapons of calibre higher than 12.7 millimetre. That was the ban in force at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom? Imposed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a result, like all the other truces, cease-fires, that were signed, this was the result of the efforts of the UN. And both sides had signed this as an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you said that -- could you tell us more about -- you answered to one of my questions that a team was established on the order of the commander. Who participated in that team, the team that would have to ascertain whether the mortar shell came from your positions? Who participated in that team?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that team, there is an order that the commander issued. In that team, there was Colonel Cvetkovic was a member of that team. And there was another member of that team. But this was an order to establish a mixed team, a joint team. That's what I spoke of yesterday. But our two members --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to be quite clear. I asked you whether there was a team within your corps, so not your delegations to a mixed team but whether there was a team investigating the incident without the participation of either international or members of the opposite forces.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would not be able to answer this question. I don't know. I only know about what I told you a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You know about the mixed team and that it failed to perform. You told us that finally you did not participate because the UNPROFOR could not guarantee your safety. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ask for any guarantees, or did they say, "you cannot come because it's too unsafe"? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. What I do know is that the response from the UNPROFOR command was that those members of the mixed team cannot be guaranteed safety in the territory under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was finally on the basis of this message of UNPROFOR that your forces were not able to participate in an investigation, a mixed team. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I presume that the commander did not wish to risk sending his men to death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You told us about what a person by the name of Demurenko said about the Markale market incident. Did you hear that from his own mouth, or was it hearsay for you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: His interview that was given to the Associated Press agency was carried by all most important media houses in the whole world. And this interview lasted for 18 minutes. And it is in this way that I found out about his results, or rather, about his findings. That's how I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it televised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that was carried by all the media houses, both newspaper and television, and also our television, in the world and in our country, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was then -- at that time already broadcasted, or did you see it later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the event, I'm not sure exactly how long after, but say after a fortnight, perhaps 20 days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shortly after the event. These were my questions. Is there any need to put additional questions to the witness in respect of issues that have been -- yes. At least Judge Nieto-Navia has an additional question. Any of the parties as well? No. Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Serbian army or the SRK in particular used or had dum dum bullets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Such type of ammunition, ammunition, wasn't in the possession even of the former JNA. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Assuming the Defence doesn't have any questions, may I be allowed to ask just a couple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they arise from the examination by the Bench, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said you were shot at by the barracks at Lukavica. Where were the barracks you were shot at?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that, sir. That was in the barracks area, and if you wish, I can show it to you on the map. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 18518 to 18525.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Mr. President. Mentioning this sniping incident does not come from the questions asked by your Chamber. It has already been asked before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the location came from the Chamber, whereas the event as such was asked by the examination of the parties. So if it is about the location, I would consider that you may ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I'm trying to ask you, sir, is where exactly, in which building, if a building, or where exactly in the barracks compound were you at when you were shot at?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in an open space. I was on one of the internal roads in the compound near a portion of elevated ground. And it was called Vranjis. That's inside the compound of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked a few questions about the Markale incident. Do you remember the date of it, the date of the incident you were speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the month of the incident you were speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to recall precisely. I think it was in August, or perhaps even July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the year of the incident you were speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1995. If we are speaking of Markale II.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just inquire of the Court, you had asked some questions in respect of Markale. And it might well be that he was answering questions in respect of a different incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, I described the incident as a shell falling on the Markale market. That was the incident I was talking about. Since you now say Markale II --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There were two incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would you call Markale I? You said Markale II in answering a question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was one incident similar to this one. But that was in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When we were talking about a mixed investigation, at least plans to establish a group, a mixed group, joint group, to investigate the incident, did that happen on both incidents or just on the incidents you had a mind when answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in relation -- I'm sorry. I apologise. That was in relation to Markale I at the time when General Galic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you answered my questions, and when I referred to your answer in the beginning of my questions, your answer about Markale investigation, did you always have Markale I in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked questions about Markale I, but not about Markale II. Do you know the date of the -- or the month of the incident you had in mind when answering my questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the exact date, but I think it was in July. I think it was in July. Or perhaps August, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many questions do you still have, Mr. Stamp? Because we are close to the time when we have to finish because of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps I could put it to the Court first, because it is not a question that directly arises out of what the Court asked. I would ask for leave to put it. Although I would still submit that a reply from -- of some new matters that my friend inquired in regular examination. It is just to describe exactly where this steel and slab barrier was in relation to the soldiers' quarters and the commander's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you briefly describe the steel slab you talked about between the office building and the officers' club, and could you, for me, tell as well, how high that was. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I just wanted to point out that this does not arise from the questions put by your Chamber, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware of that. But if you would have a look at my notes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and if you could look into my mind, you would have found out that where I put in my notes that I had to ask further details about the steel slab, I had forgotten. So consider it to be an additional question by the Bench. Could you please tell us more in detail where the steel slab was and how high it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I point it out on the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We know that there is certain distance between the building and the -- was it in the middle of the open space or was it closer to the office building? Was it closer to the soldiers' club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we remember the video, between the soldiers' club and the command building, there's an empty space. There is a lawn which is about 15 metres wide. So that entire area between those two buildings, there were steel slabs in that area. And they were about as high as the first floor. They reached to the first floor more or less. But perhaps those slabs, the height of the slabs, was 2 metres. And an entire belt was covered by those slabs between the military club building, and the building in which General Galic had his office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my clarification, when you say approximately 2 metres, would that mean from the first floor, you would look over a steel slab?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. Those slabs, the dimensions of which were about 2 by 2, they were on wooden supports. And at the level of the windows of the first floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have a better understanding. Well, you've answered now all the questions from the parties and from the Bench. I'd like to thank you for doing that and for coming to The Hague. We all know it's a long distance. And we hope that you have a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And with your permission, I would just like to conclude by greeting my commander, and I would like to thank you and I hope that our cooperation has been fruitful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'll adjourn, I would say, until 5.30, and I would ask whether it would be possible, then, for the interpreters and the technical assistants to then continue without a break until 7.00. Would that be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That's acceptable for the interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE INTERPERTER: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll find out during the break whether there's any technical difficulty in achieving it. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If you could look into my mind, then one would have noticed that this question could have been put to General Galic, too. I know that he is more ill than we are on occasion. And it would be good to ask him whether he can support this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I always expect you, General Galic, to interfere when your health situation would not allow to follow what is suggested. So if that would be the case, please tell us. And if not, let's then quickly enjoy our break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good day. Or good evening. Well, it will be difficult for me, I have to say SO, but I do have my medicine, and I will try to bear with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it would comfort you to make it 40 or 45 minutes, we will do so. But if you say 35 minutes will do, then...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the current break is not at issue, but the length of the proceedings. If I can just stand up, I'll do so, then I could sit down again. And everything will be all right then. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's good for you just to stand for a couple of minutes, then please ask and we'll permit you, and we'll explain to whoever will be the witness that it's for your health. If we can accommodate you, we'll gladly do so. Then we'll adjourn until 5.30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if you would guide us through the documents, and at the same time I do understand that there's a slight change in the order of appearance of the witnesses, that is to say that the witness Indjic will be the next one to testify since he really has to leave before the weekend. The Chamber still hopes and thinks that both witness DP2 and witness Indjic could be examined until Friday, quarter to 2.00. Could the witness be stand by so that he can enter the courtroom immediately after we have gone through the documents. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The first document is D719, and that is a regular military report dated the 25th of June, 1993. The next document is D542, which is also a regular military report dated 12th of March, 1994. The next document is D1235. That is also a document, a military report, dated the 7th of November, 1992. The next exhibit is D935, which is a regular military report dated the 5th of August, 1993. There is a map marked by the witness, D1838. And there's two separate sheets, to make one map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it not be a practical way that we combine them into one sheet. So although it exists of two parts now, 1838, the Chamber will combine them so that they are one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to the Defence exhibits, the Prosecution adopts the usual position which is that only those parts of the military reports and similar documents which were the subject of examination be entered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next document is D825, and that is a regular military report dated the 11th of July, 1993. Another document, D1144, and that is a regular military report dated the 13th of November, 1993. D1631 is the next document, and that is dated the 9th of January, 1994. D588, which is a regular daily report, and that is dated the 17th of April, 1993. D837, that is a regular military report dated the 24th of July, 1993. D1035, and that is a regular military report dated the 3rd of September, 1993. D864, regular military report dated the 22nd of July, 1994. D861, regular military report dated July 17th, 1994. D741, regular military report dated the 19th of June, 1994. D748, that is a regular military report dated the 26th of June, 1994. D735, which is a regular military report dated the 13th of June, 1994. D1111, and this is a regular military report dated the 7th of October, 1993. The next exhibit is D1108, regular military report dated the 4th of October, 1993. D543, regular military report dated the 13th of March, 1994. And there's two more. D1039, regular military report dated the 7th of September, 1993. And the last one is D936, which is a regular military report dated the 6th of August, 1993. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I noticed that each of the regular military reports, a partial translation of the document is attached, that is, the heading and usually the full paragraph which we find under number 1, and the very end of the report, signature, date, et cetera. So they are attached to it, and they are part of the document as tendered and as now admitted into evidence unless Mr. Piletta-Zanin would withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I just wanted to add something with regard to what the Prosecution said. In general, in these documents, there are stamps which certify in addition to their authenticity, which has been confirmed by the witness, it certifies the fact that these orders were distributed. They were addressed to someone, they were forwarded to someone. There was a sender and a receiver. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether they were forwarded or not is, I think, not in evidence, but at least I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that the Defence takes the position that if a letter contains the one who sent it and the one to whom it is addressed, that you would take it for acceptable that they have been sent. I didn't hear any objection from the Prosecution. I take it that where the stamps are a legible part, even without translation, and since mention has been made of these stamps several times by the witness, that at least in these photocopies, the stamps as they appear are part of the document that is admitted into evidence, then. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what I want to say is that this is not what we are assuming. This stamp is proof that these orders were distributed. And as such, they were recorded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if a stamp on a photocopy would prove what you say now, I'm not saying it's not proved. I didn't hear any objection. But this position seems not in every respect to correspond with the position previously taken a few times by the Defence in respect of photocopy documents and stamps on that. But it's not -- I didn't hear any objection, so the Chamber will -- yes, Mr. Stamp. Apart from you objected in general terms at the beginning that -- not objecting against the admission of the document now does not mean that the Prosecution accepts them to be true copies of the originals. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As to be authentic, yes, true copies of the originals. And I should add, if the Court would be prepared to receive them, we are prepared to provide our draft translations of the complete documents. I notice the President had mentioned the issue of translations, or parts of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, until now -- usually the parties are required to translate as much as necessary to understand a part of a document in its context. We have been provided with translations of paragraph 1. Questions, but not specifically to the content, but in more general terms have been put to the witness in respect of paragraph 2 which we could not verify. And if the Prosecution would provide translations and request that they would be admitted in order to create the context of the document, we'll then consider that matter once the request is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is the Defence ready to call its next witness? Yes, I see you are nodding yes, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the limitations that were just explained, until now, the documents are admitted into evidence, that means in respect of those parts on which the witness was examined, in respect of the paragraphs 1, the headings, and the end of the document. And as far as general questions have been put to the witness in respect of the paragraphs 2, that part as such is then in evidence. I take it that you are Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, before giving evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. And I'd like to invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Indjic, please be seated. You'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence. Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, could you tell us your full name and your date of birth and place.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Indjic. I was born in Sarajevo on the 1st of April in 1957.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what rank you hold at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: At the moment, I am Lieutenant-Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were born on the 1st of April, 1957, in Sarajevo. Can you tell us how long you lived there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I more or less spent my entire life in Sarajevo apart from a few years, which I spent when I was studying outside of Sarajevo. That was four years of secondary school. If necessary, I can say this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you to provide us with more details about your education, but my question was up until when did you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo up until the time of the Dayton agreement, up until when the Dayton agreement was signed, when part of Sarajevo was -- became part of the Federation in accordance with the Dayton agreement. My flat was in that area, and that's when I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in order to be more precise, can you tell us which part of Sarajevo you lived in up until the time when you left the city.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I lived in the part of Sarajevo called Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we started talking about the area you lived in, you mentioned your absence from Sarajevo, the period during which you were absent from Sarajevo, and you said that was while you were attending schools. Which schools have you finished? What's your educational background?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I finished primary school, the air force and military secondary school in Mostar in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, please speak slowly for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: So secondary school in 1975, and then the technical air force academy in Rajlovac. I finished my studies there in 1978. In 1981, I finished the JNA school for foreign languages in Belgrade. And in 1986, I completed an intelligence course in Pancevo. In addition to those schools, I commenced post-graduate studies in political sciences in Zagreb. I didn't complete these studies because the war broke out in Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us about the schools you completed. But which professional duties did you have until the conflict in Sarajevo broke out and in the course of the conflict in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can answer this question in two ways. I can talk about the breakout of the conflict. When I finished the academy, I worked as a platoon commander in the secondary military school in Rajlovac. And then I worked as a teacher in the secondary military school and the technical air force academy in Rajlovac. In February 1992, I was assigned as a liaison officer in the group for cooperation with UNPROFOR. It was a group from the former JNA. From that period, up until the end of the war in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the duties I performed were those of the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Indjic, as far as I have understood, you were the liaison officer while the JNA, the former JNA army, still existed. And you told me that later on, you also performed this -- these duties, the duties of the liaison officer. Within which army did you perform these duties and where?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: If I have understood your question correctly, it only refers to the second period. So I will focus on this period alone. When the group for cooperating with the United Nations was disbanded, the former JNA group, I was assigned to a group which cooperate we had UNPROFOR which belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska. I was assigned to that group by the order of the federal secretariat of national defence of the former SRJ. And it was my desire to stay within the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina because that's where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
