utterances.text: Thank you. If I have understood you, you were a liaison officer in the group for cooperating with UNPROFOR which functioned within the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what your role in that group was? How many of there were there in that group and did you have any particular function?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Since it took a certain amount of time for this group to be formed, just as it took some time for the Army of Republika Srpska to be formed, at the very beginning, the group wasn't fully staffed, and there were only three men who were performing duties there. In addition to me, Colonel Zarkovic and my colleague Luledzija [Realtime transcript read in error "Lugonja"] were in that group. The duties I had in the group were those of a liaison officer. And Colonel Zarkovic headed the group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think the surname Luledzija has been entered into the transcript. It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, could you spell that, given your knowledge of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: May I suggest that perhaps my learned colleague and the witness might slow down. It's a cracking pace, and that probably explains why the name wasn't caught. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I ask you to speak a bit more slowly, Mr. Indjic, because the interpreters really have problems in following your speed of language. Please proceed. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And likewise, I would like to ask Mr. Ierace, if he has to intervene, to wait for the interpretation to finish. Since some people are still listening to it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may address the Chamber if you want to express your disagreement with the way Mr. Ierace behaves. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I will continue. But the surname in the transcript is now Lugonja. I think this should be corrected to avoid any confusion later on. The witness said Luledzija. I could ask Mr. Indjic to spell Mr. Luledzija's surname, for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please spell the name you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] LUDZ -- L-U-L-E-D-Z-I-J-A.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, can you briefly tell us what your duties were as the liaison officer after you had been assigned to the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The main duties of the group of liaison officers, and that included myself as a member of that group of the liaison officers, the main duties were to serve as a link between the warring factions, or the representatives of the international community and the Army of Republika Srpska. It was to facilitate communication between these factions. And when I say communication, I mean that through our group, our liaison group, all requests, various requests, various documents would be received, and they would be forwarded to the people they were intended for and vice versa. This also included all essential technical preparations needed to organise meetings at various levels. It included the participation of interpreters at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you also mentioned dealing with all requests and all the documents that arose that you would receive while on duty. With reference to that period, that is to say, after the formation of your group, or to be more precise, from September 1992 up until August 1994, with regard to those requests, did you receive documents that were, in fact, protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us what your duties were in the liaison group, the group for cooperation. Can you tell us whether in the course of a working day, let's take one of your working days as an example. In the course of such a day, did you plan your activities? Did you make a plan?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It was almost impossible to make a daily, weekly, or monthly plan of our activities because our activities depended on the work and the requests of others. And it was, in fact, the purpose of our office to provide services to these others. Usually, we would only make daily plans for our activities after which we would examine what had been planned, what had been ordered, what was necessary to do, and we would examine these matters at a morning meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you explained what your duties were, what your role was, and what your cooperation or liaison group did. Can you tell us what was your authority within that group? That is, did you, as a liaison officer, did you have the right to decide, to take decisions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No. Like in any other army in the world, the person who is carrying out the duties of a liaison officer does not have any possibility to decide on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, speaking of your work within that group, in relation to UNPROFOR and humanitarian activities, so to speak, did you, as a liaison officer, have the authority to decide about when and where, in which direction, would a humanitarian convoy go through the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the delivery of a humanitarian aid, and particularly about the convoys of humanitarian aid, the authority to approve these convoys, it was -- it -- the authority was with the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Even the corps commander was not able to approve the passage of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, this was ordered in written form by the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. And there was a specifically established procedure to advise of and approve humanitarian convoy passages.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you just told us that there was an order, in fact, order given by the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. When we're talking about movement and approval of movement of vehicles of UNPROFOR, humanitarian vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, considering that the witness spoke of this order of the main staff of the VRS, the Defence would like to present the witness with a document. We have disclosed this document to the Prosecution. And with your leave, would like to show it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, could you please assist Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, perhaps my learned colleague could confirm that this document will -- perhaps clarify this document was on the exhibit list or whether it was disclosed for the first time -- and whether it was disclosed for the first time a few days ago, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was received by the Defence from Mr. Indjic. And I told my learned colleague that I received a copy of this document, and that's why I disclosed it in due course. It is not on the exhibit list of the Defence, but this is the document that the Defence received only a couple of days ago. And we did inform our learned colleagues about this. This document has the number of 1839. And I propose that it be made part of the exhibits as they come. And the copy of that document and the translation of the document, I have disclosed to my learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have any objection to the document being shown to the witness. I think just as a matter of course, one should seek leave to rely on a document which hasn't been disclosed under reciprocal disclosure, and especially not included on the exhibit list. But I have no objection to it in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the order of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, which was forwarded to all the subordinate corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, this document which is before you, is this the document that you have given to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, under Item 5 of this document, does it say -- is there a provision which regulates the work of the liaison officers?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This provision confirms what it says about the movement of humanitarian convoys, that is, it clears up the approval of the movement of the convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read Item 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Approval of movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid convoys cannot be performed orally by phone, but exclusively by written documents of the main staff of the VRS and the corps command. Liaison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you for a second. On the video evidence screen, nothing appears. So there must be a technical problem, I take it. It has been fixed? It's being fixed. If you would have any question apart from this document, because, Ms. Pilipovic, for the public character of the trial, it would be good to be able to have this document a public character as well. Or could the technical booth inform us about how much time it would still take. Since we have no idea, if you have any questions not related to the document to be shown on the ELMO, Ms. Pilipovic, you could first ask these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, could you tell us whether your duties as a liaison officer, did they go over the SRK field, that is, did you perform any duties for any other organs or commands?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the establishment of the group of liaison with UNPROFOR, the only possible communication between the UNPROFOR command for the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and the command for the Sarajevo sector with the Army of Republika Srpska was through the office, liaison office, of our group. And it was for that reason to start with, the beginning of our work, the scope of our duties occasionally did go over the area of responsibility of the SRK, of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. As time went on, this problem was resolved because UNPROFOR created their own group of liaison officers in Pale, and they kept contact with the main staff. And that part of the work was no longer within our authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you said liaison office. Can you tell us, during those initial stages, I understand that there were two parts that you are talking about. So during this initial stage when you had much wider authority outside of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, can you tell us where were your offices? And when you say "in the beginning," can you tell us when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In the initial stage, that is, from the beginning when the war, conflict, broke out, a need was created to have a communication between the warring sides and the international community, that is, and the peacekeeping forces with the warring sides. It was for this reason that it was agreed that offices of liaison offices would be opened for all three warring sides at the UNPROFOR command in the PTT building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the ELMO is working again. So if you need to return to the document, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, the document that you have on your right, that is before you, you said this was the document of the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska which was sent to the command and also to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Can you please read item 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Approval of movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid convoys cannot be given orally by phone, but exclusively through written documents of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and the corps command. Liaison officers with UNPROFOR do not have the authority to approve the movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid convoys."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Indjic, can you tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This document was signed by the chief of staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated 6th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the type of document in relation to the approval of UNPROFOR like you mentioned before?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were several warnings and documents about the authority to approve movement of convoys.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I do not know whether the translation of the document, but if you look at the English text as to who signed this document, are there any...? Well, let's say the Chamber is divided in its opinion on who signed the document in English. I can tell you that Judge Nieto-Navia has Brigadier General Manojlo Milovanovic, whereas the Presiding Judge has --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've made a mistake. Yes, I'm aware of that. The second document, when I was putting them together, I attached a different page of the document. When I see what's on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You think you made a mistake. But the Chamber was provided with different documents as far as the English translation is concerned. I've got Stanislav Galic as the one who signed the document. And it's a bit shorter as well, mine. So there are...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that the Defence was going to show the witness, 1840, the second page of that document has obviously been mistakenly attached as a translation for this original. I think that is what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think to some of the documents, because we have different versions within the Chamber. I think I got the wrong one, and my colleagues have the right one, I take it. Could you at least provide the Presiding Judge, and let's check with the Prosecution, do you have a document of which the second page --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, we've got the correct one, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll return the wrong one to you, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a sufficient number of copies of translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We require another one because the copy given to the witness was the wrong one as well, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps with your leave, Your Honour, I can prepare that copy for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I please check the... Ms. Pilipovic, you again provided a wrong translation. Could you please provide a second page in the translation numbered 6789 with the signature of Milovanovic, and not, as you did again, an unnumbered second page with the signature of General Galic in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, but the last name and the signature are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, they aren't. They were not in the previous version you gave us. Yes, now we've got the right one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, so on this document, you said that the document was signed by Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic, chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just before we looked at this document, we were talking about the period before the conflict broke out, and that your offices were in the PTT building as a liaison officer in the group with the liaison with UNPROFOR and the warring parties. Can you tell us precisely, when you say from the beginning of the conflict, can you give us a date and also until when were you in the PTT building with your -- that was the location for your premises?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I think that the premises at the PTT building were established at the end of May for all the three parties in the armed conflict in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the office of the liaison officer of the Army of Republika Srpska was operational until September 1992 when there was a suspension.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that the offices were operational until September 1992, and that when you say that there was a suspension, this suspension, was it in relation to the arrival of General Galic as the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No. It was caused by physical threats addressed to us that myself and the colleague who was with me in the office and who was representing the civilian authorities, Dr. Vlado Lukic, later on he was the prime minister of the Republika Srpska government, that we would be killed. These threats were addressed to us by a famous Sarajevo criminal, Samir Kahvedzic, also known as Krusko. And this was feasible realistically speaking because the office was located on the ground floor of that facility, and on that side the facility was not secured by UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, can you tell us where were your premises, if you had them, and where were they located after that suspension, that is, starting from September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: After the withdrawal from the PTT building, the office was established in the part of the building where the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was, or more precisely, in the left wing of that building. Opposite the part of the building where the operations room was and the commander's office. They were in the right wing of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Indjic, your offices from September were located in the building of the command in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Except that after a series of talks with the sector -- Sarajevo sector commander and the guarantee given on the question of security of liaison officers at the UNPROFOR command, later on, after a certain period, the office was again opened at the PTT building, although I personally did not go back there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you personally did not go back there to the PTT building, did you have a contact from your office at Lukavica? Did you have a contact with the office at the PTT building? And if you did, what kind of contact was that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: We had a permanent, 24-hour contact between Lukavica office at the -- and the PTT building office. This was a telephone contact, and it was used only for routine matters because the telephone cable went across the territory under enemy control. And therefore, the conversations were monitored and other types of communication, and that was necessary which was the actual direct arrival of liaison officers to the command to Lukavica. He would be brought by UNPROFOR members. And if he needed deliver some mail or be given some instructions for further work, he would then come himself to the Lukavica building command.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, when you told us that you did not have the authority as a liaison officer to approve movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid, as far as I've understood, without the approval of the superior organ, you were not able to take certain decisions. Did I understand you correctly that you did not have -- you did not have the authority to resolve any request at the Sarajevo Romanija Corps as a liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Not me personally, or any other member of the group, liaison group, with UNPROFOR, who was on duty as a liaison officer. None of us had any authority to, on our own authority, decide or resolve something or approve anything on our own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, since you're telling us about the cooperation with UNPROFOR, can you tell us, in relation to that part of the duties, that is, cooperation with UNPROFOR, what kind of requests did you receive from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Most of the requests that came from UNPROFOR were related to the approval of various kinds of movement, whether convoys, humanitarian aid, or changing shifts of units. The second kind of requests was asking for approval to -- for assistance during various humanitarian missions and repairs to infrastructures. Electricity, network, water or gas, and similar. Another kind of request that we received, these were requests related to the organisation of meetings on -- at various levels.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that one type of request that you received from UNPROFOR was organisation at various levels, organisation of meetings at various levels, can you tell us what kind of meetings were there and at what levels?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In order to establish good cooperation with United Nations representatives, in Republika Srpska and also in the Army of Republika Srpska, at various levels there were organs, bodies, that were established. And they were responsible for this kind of cooperation. At the political level, a committee for cooperation with United Nations representatives, was established, and this was led by late Professor Nikola Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. The level of the Army of Republika Srpska matters were discussed by a joint working group. This mixed or joint working group encompassed representatives of main staffs of the warring parties and UNPROFOR representatives. A lower level was a joint military commission, joint military commissions were established, I believe, in 1993. And they encompassed the corps level. Meetings at lower levels were generally not held.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you told us that at the level of the Army of Republika Srpska, in that army, a working group was formed. And representatives of the warring factions and UNPROFOR representatives participated in it. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. A mixed working group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, do you personally know anything about the work of that mixed working group within the army of Republika Srpska? And if you do know anything about this, were you present at these meetings, and who was present, who represented -- who represented the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the work of this mixed working group because as liaison officer, because of the organisation of the meeting, because of interpreting at those meetings, I was present at almost all the meetings of this body unless I was absent for private reasons at the time. Various issues were discussed at these meetings, issues of a general nature. And representatives of the main staffs of the warring factions were present. If the result of the negotiations of those representatives resulted in the signing of some kind of agreement, then at a meeting at which the agreement would be signed, the chiefs of the main staffs of the warring factions would attend these meetings in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Indjic. We will also talk about agreements and the agreements that were signed later on. But I'm now interested in that mixed working group. In the command of the corps of the SRK, were there such meetings with UNPROFOR representatives? And do you personally know anything about those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: As I said, there were joint military commissions at the corps level, and these commissions were bodies that had to put into operation what had been agreed on at the meetings of mixed working groups. And this then had to be put in an order for the cause. And the meetings of these joint mixed commissions would be held in neutral territory. Usually this was at the Sarajevo airport which was under the control of the French battalion, which was part of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, have I understood you correctly, what was agreed between the warring factions and with UNPROFOR at the level of that mixed working group, with regard to what had to be implemented at a later stage, you had commissions within the organisation of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the purpose of which was to implement what had been agreed at the level of the mixed working group, at the level of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The joint working commission at the level of the corps did implement and put into operation what had been agreed at the level of the main staff. And at these joint military commissions, they didn't even raise new issues. If it was necessary to discuss at the level of the corps about a new issue, then this would be suggested -- it would be suggested to the working group, to the military working group, that it should first discuss the matter and adopt positions with regard to these matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the witness's answers, the Defence wants to show the witness two documents. It's Document D1656 and Document 1655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which of the documents you would like to have first on the ELMO, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 1655.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, would you please first return the other document to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you have document D1655 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of document this is. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a regular combat report from the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps addressed to the main staff of the Republika Srpska army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The document is dated the 5th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read item 2 in this document.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: "A meeting of the mixed group is ongoing organised by UNPROFOR, and our team is being led by the chief of staff -- is headed by the chief of staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, do you have Document 1656 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that the witness only read the last two lines of item 2? I don't know whether your question has been properly translated. Did you ask the witness to read item 2 or to read the last two lines of item 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last two lines of item 2. I said paragraph 2 of item 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's clear to us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you have Document 1656 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also a regular combat report with the situation at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out paragraphs 3 and 4 of item 2.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: A meeting of the mixed group was held organised by UNPROFOR. Three issues were discussed. Opening up humanitarian corridors, demilitarising the Sarajevo area, establishing air corridors.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Indjic, can you tell us whether these are the tasks of the mixed group which held meetings at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: These are tasks which would be put into operation at the corps level, but they would be agreed at the level of the mixed working group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you attended those meetings. And you told us about your role. Can you tell us whether those meetings were also held in the period from September 1992 until August 1994? And if so, how frequently were they held?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Meetings were, as a rule, held quite regularly. I could even say that once a month or once every six weeks, but this was not the case during periods when the fighting was intense, and I can say quite freely, during periods that nothing other owner the war functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, can you tell us at those meetings when main staffs of -- when representatives of the main staffs from both warring factions were present, can you tell us whether the problem, the issue of shelling was discussed at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings, were the military activities of both sides discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The issues that were discussed and that had to do with military activities was there to do with attempts to put an end to military action, at least for a certain period of time, if not completely. Or rather, they had to do with attempting to reach a cease-fire agreement, attempting to establish a truce.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that I have understood your answer, at those meetings, they would discuss agreements on cease-fires? They would discuss respecting truces?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would discuss establishing and respecting truces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At those meetings of the mixed military group, since UNPROFOR representatives were also present, was the issue of protests discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As a liaison officer, can you tell us whether you received protests from UNPROFOR at your post at Lukavica, and if you did, what form did these protests take?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive protests in our office, and they were sent to us in a written and in a verbal form.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say a written and verbal form, I'll first of all ask you about verbal protests. How many verbal protests were made in the course of one month or in the course of a day?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to answer this question because it wasn't the same throughout all the periods. When there was a truce and the truce was respected, there were very few protests or there were none at all. And this was not the case when the fighting was intense and during periods when the fighting was intense. It's very difficult for me to answer your question precisely to tell you how many such protests there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, which form of protest was more frequent, written ones or oral ones?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: If I could put this in terms of percentage, 95 per cent of the protests were written protests. There were far more --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, could you please repeat your last answer. It was -- the question was: Which form of protests was more frequent, written ones or oral ones? Could you please repeat what you answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Verbal protests were more frequent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you have told us that verbal protests were more frequent, can you briefly tell us how these verbal protests were made by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I have to explain that within the UNPROFOR structure, there were various levels which were in a position to lodge protests. For example, there were the UN military observers. That was one level. There were liaison officers from UNPROFOR battalions. That was a second level. There was the command of the Sarajevo sector, the UNPROFOR command of the Sarajevo sector. That would be the third level. And then the fourth level would be the UNPROFOR command for the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. The majority of verbal protests came from the UN military observers and from liaison officers from the UNPROFOR battalion who were located in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, when you say that the majority of the verbal protests - and we are talking about verbal protests - when you say that you received the majority of these protests, such protests from UN observers, can you tell us whether you personally received all these protests, and if so, can you tell us who processed these protests? Who dealt with them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Well, just for the sake of clarity, I'd like to repeat that you can't equate the group for cooperation with UNPROFOR and Indjic Milenko. It's not the same thing. I was just one of the liaison officers in that group. So it would be more appropriate to say that the protests were sent via the group for the cooperation with UNPROFOR. And whether that concerned myself or one of my colleagues, that is irrelevant. But when we received protests from the military observers, and the conditions they had were the best for lodging protests because our offices were more or less next to each other, only 2 metres separated our offices, they had channels of communication which were open 24 hours a day, when we received a protest, we would examine to see whether all the essential elements of the protest were there in order for us to be able to respond. And let me clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, we will return to clarification -- the matter of clarifying the protests that you received in your office from UN military observers. If I understood you correctly they were in the same building you were located in?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I just want this to be clearer. You said that the protests from liaison officers of the battalion and of the sector command for Sarajevo, and you said for the command for Bosnia and Herzegovina, you mentioned these protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the written or verbal form of these protests, were they also directed to your office? Did you receive them in your office, and who processed those protests? We're talking about four categories of protests. Let's go back to the first group?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It all went through the office of the liaison officers, any communication from UNPROFOR, including protests. So it wasn't possible for such protests to be sent to someone in the corps command in another way. It wasn't possible to bypass the office of the liaison officers. The protests received would be sent, would be forwarded to the duty officer in the corps command, and the duty officer, after performing the duties that he had to perform, would inform the commander of the protest. And if the commander wasn't present, then he would inform the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If we're talking about the protests to the -- from the command for Bosnia and Herzegovina, did you receive such protests, and did you forward them and deal with these protests in a similar way?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Protests from the UNPROFOR commander of Bosnia and Herzegovina were always addressed to the main staff of the Republika Srpska army. They were usually protests which were in a written form, and it was our duty to forward that protest as rapidly as possible to the main staff of the Republika Srpska army. The situation was made easier, as I've already said, when an UNPROFOR office for liaison officers was established in Pale, and they took over those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said that most of the verbal protests were ones that you received from UN observers, can you tell us what the contents of those protests was, the protests that, as you said, you forwarded to the duty officer in the corps command?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: To make things a little clearer, I'll just briefly say that the UN military observers were deployed at observation posts on both sides of the front line. Their commands were in the corps commands, and they were called HQ Lima and HQ Papa. The military observers usually only forwarded the protests made by one of the warring factions, and they forwarded to the other warring faction through its channels of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, to the extent that I have understood your answer, if you, as the duty officer, received a verbal protest from UN members, you are saying that they would be relaying you protests made by a warring faction. In this particular case, it would be a protest made by the BH army. Can you tell us what the contents of those protests were? And you have told us that it was usually a protest made by one of the warring factions. What were the contents of the protests that you would receive? We're still talking about verbal protests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected, Mr. President, but the question just asked referred to protests by the BH army, I think implying that the witness had said that. I don't know that the witness has said that. Perhaps that might be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But didn't the witness make a distinction --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said the warring factions, and I provided that as an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness made a distinction --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Ms. Pilipovic, could you please conclude in --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness just answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Indjic, my question was what were the contents of the verbal protests that a UN observer would forward to you? And you said that these were mostly protests made by one of the warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The protests mostly had to do with the alleged violation of the truce, or perhaps with action taken in certain areas. On the whole, we took each protest very seriously. The first thing that had to be done was to determine whether the protest was complete in order to see whether any action could be taken on the basis of the protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, we'll stop at that point. You said see whether the protest was complete. We will have a break now, and then you can continue with your analysis and tell us what else had to be done when you received a protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Indjic, may I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given in this Court until now and you're still about to give. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we expect you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Just very briefly, the French booth, battalions, and not a battalion. The witness was speaking in the plural. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a reference as far as line and page are concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not exactly, Mr. President. I heard it a while ago, but we'll certainly find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that would certainly assist those who are working on the transcript at night. May I urge the parties, not because it's not going the right way, but we are all informed that the present witness would like to leave before the weekend. So therefore, if full efficiency could be achieved, we might be able to achieve that. Could I ask the specific attention of the parties to it especially because the Chamber would not like to be put in a position where we had to hurry up with our own questions, if we would have any. So may I ask the cooperation of the parties. Then we'll adjourn until 9.00, tomorrow morning. Same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
